To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we discovered a MAT1‐ 2 locus from a P. chrysogenum wild‐type strain, which is functional in sexual development, and that mating between the MAT1‐1 strain and the newly isolated MAT1‐2 isolate generated sexual spores, indicating that the wild type can be used as a donor in strain improvement programs.

the MAT1‐1 and MAT1‐2 mating‐type locuses are functional in the wild‐type strain of Penicillium, and that sexual spores were generated by crossing a MAT1‐ 2 wild‐type strain with a MAT1-1 industrial penicillin‐producer.

we identified a functional MAT1‐2 mating‐type locus in a Penicillium wild‐type strain, characterized its function, sequenced the parental strain and progeny, and found evidence of recombination in the progeny.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of mating‐type gene function in the penicillium model system and its potential application to industrial strain improvement.
the sexual life cycle of P. chrysogenum and its potential application for strain improvement in industrial penicillin‐producers.
the elucidation of the sexual cycle of P. chrysogenum and with the application of sexual reproduction to strain improvement.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the MAT1‐1 strain has the ability to produce more antibiotics than the MAT1-2 strain.
the sexual stage in P. chrysogenum can contribute to industrial strain improvement.
the MAT1–2 locus has a function beyond sexual development.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that MAT genes are not only important for sexual development but also for asexual development and that the MAT genes can be used to generate new strains for industrial applications.

we discovered a new MAT1‐2‐like wild-type strain, we characterized the mating-type locus, we performed mating of this strain with the MAT1‐1 industrial strain and we performed whole genome sequencing of the progeny strains.
we have shown the feasibility of mating of industrial strains of Penicillium and that this can be achieved by using wild‐type strains as a mating partner.
The main takeaway from our work is that
mating‐type genes can be used for strain improvement in industrial fungi, which is a novel approach in industrial microbiology.
the mating system of P. chrysogenum can be harnessed to generate new strains with desired phenotypes.
the MAT1–2 locus is a powerful tool to study the sexual life cycle in P. chrysogenum, and it can be used to improve penicillin production.
